highlights.text: smallness and lowliness/contemptibility
al-ṣāghir is one who accepts being wronged or subjected (ḍaym)
a low one (iṣghār) and a loud one (ikbār)
al-Rāghib defines al-ṣaghw as inclining (al-mayl)
The stars and the sun are said to ṣaghā when they incline toward setting
and so that the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter may incline toward it
two separate original meanings of the same root, unified only by the shared consonantal form
The verb sahara means to melt something
The noun al-sihr means al-khatan, a relation acquired through marriage
praising someone as one who "melted" (tested/subdued) boys/youths as no one else could
two things meeting with force and vehemence
ṣakaktu al-shayʾ ṣakkan: "I struck the thing."
jiʾtuhu ṣakkata ʿumayyin, "I came to him at ʿumayy's collision"
الصَّلاَح (ṣalāḥ) means "soundness / being in good and right order," the opposite of فَسَاد (corruption, spoiling)
Zabīdī notes a scholarly dispute over whether prophets may be described by ṣalāḥ: the base view restricts it to ordinary people, while al-Subkī and others allowed it of prophets too
One who is sound is ṣilḥ, ṣāliḥ, or ṣalīḥ; one who actively sets things right is مُصْلِح (muṣliḥ)
his good deeds (ṣāliḥāt) are beyond count
أَصْلَحَ (aṣlaḥa), "to set right / repair," the opposite of أَفْسَدَ (afsada, "to spoil")
الصُّلْح (ṣulḥ), "reconciliation, peace-making" between parties
Shāhid: Bishr b. Abī Khāzim, "They seek reconciliation (ṣilāḥ) at Dhāt Kahf…,"
Shāhid: verses of Ḥarb (or al-Ḥārith) b. Umayya inviting Abū Maṭar to safety and good living at Ṣalāḥ among Quraysh
المَصْلَحة (maṣlaḥah), "benefit, public interest"; plural maṣāliḥ, contrasted with mafāsid ("harms")
dry clay that has not been fired (i.e. not baked into pottery)
The name is explained from the sound it makes: strike or tap it and it rings (ṭanna)
highlights.note: entry's note on the word's naming

highlights.text: two independent roots: one meaning hardness and strength, the other a kind of grease or fat (wadak)
The back (ẓahr) is called ṣulb because of its strength
the maṣlūb (the one crucified/impaled) was named from this second root — as though fat were running down his face
Cited from al-Nābigha: herded livestock spending the day beside "a ṣalīb set up on al-Zawrāʾ."
He cites a ḥadīth that when the Messenger of God saw such a figure on a garment he cut it out (qaḍabahu)
One core meaning: hardness and dryness.
al-ḥajaru al-ṣald — the hard rock
illustrated with a line of poetry by Ruʾbah
this root under two heads: burning with fire (al-ṣaly), and al-ṣalāt, which he derives mainly from supplication
al-ṣalāt means supplication, invoking blessing and glorifying
Ṣallaytu ʿalayhi means "I prayed for him and commended him"
The place of worship is also called ṣalāt, which is why churches are called ṣalawāt
The ṣalāt that is "the specific act of worship" gets its name from supplication, its root sense
highlights.note: the specific ritual act of worship

highlights.text: In his account iqāma signals that the aim is to fulfil the prayer's dues and conditions, not just to produce its outward form
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Qur'anic diction

highlights.text: He adds the reported saying: "Those who perform ṣalāt are many; those who establish it are few."
the root ص-ل-ي / ص-ل-و has two distinct origins
صَلَيْتُ العُودَ بِالنَّارِ — "I roasted/held the wood to the fire."
اصْطَلَيْتُ بِالنَّارِ — "I warmed myself at the fire."
الصَّلَى — the scorching heat of fire
Shāhid from al-Aʿshā: his daughter prays that ailments be kept from her departing father
الصَّلَاة is also what the Law (sharʿ) brought — bowing, prostration, and the rest of the ṣalāt's prescribed limits
When الصَّلَاة is ascribed to God, it means mercy (raḥma). Evidence: the ḥadīth "O God, ṣalli upon the family of Abū Awfā"
fineness/delicacy combined with compactness/being drawn together
the word for a monastic cell/tower, al-ṣawmaʿah, is derived
To head toward / aim at (al-qaṣd)
Hard, solid ground (al-ṣalāba fī al-shayʾ)
Allāh is called al-Ṣamad, Ibn Fāris explains, because His servants turn/head toward Him
boasts that at the tribe's gathering he will be found at the top of "the lofty, muṣammad tent"
a thing is closed tightly together, with no breach or opening left in it
al-ṣamam is deafness of the ear: the ear is thought of as closed
aṣmamtu al-rajula means "I found the man deaf"
highlights.note: aṣamma, 1x, so he made them deaf

highlights.text: He cites Ibn Aḥmar: "The call of my blaming woman found [me] deaf
be deaf, O daughter of the mountain!
vagueness/ambiguity and being sealed shut, extended most often to silence
ṣamata/aṣmata al-rajul — to fall silent (two verb forms)
a soft, supple coat of mail that makes no sound when worn
the making or doing of a thing
describe someone deft and expert at what they make
مَصَانِع (maṣāniʿ): structures built
a verse describing a woman "clumsy at good, but skilled (ṣanāʿ) at causing harm
He describes a ṣanam as an object fashioned out of wood, silver, or copper, which was then made an object of worship
the root signals closeness between two things
This is the image the Qur'an uses: 'and palm-trees, joined and not joined' (Qur'an 13:4)
highlights.note: ṣinwān, 2x, joined from a single root

highlights.text: He cites a line of poetry by Layla, addressed mockingly to the poet al-Nabigha and punning on his name
something falling to the ground through a struggle between two
rajul ṣarīʿ — a man thrown down
illustrated with a line of poetry about relieving hardship
something appears, stands out, becomes visible
الصَّرْح (al-ṣarḥ) is a single edifice built standing on its own, massive and rising high into the sky
Ibn Fāris cites al-Aʿshā: a dark-red wine that "discloses a redness ... when it clears after its frothing."
The root sense of al-ṣarr is gathering and binding fast.
صَرَّ يَصِرُّ صريراً / صَرْصَرَ = to make a sound, to cry at the top of the voice
صِرّ (ṣirr) and صِرّة (ṣirra) = severe cold
a single, non-repeated sound is ṣarra / ṣalla, a repeated one is ṣarṣara / ṣalṣala
Imruʾ al-Qays's line "في صَرَّةٍ لم تَزَيَّلِ" is read as "throng," as "hardship,"
in al-Nābigha's verse the ṣarūra is the monk who has renounced women
al-Zajjāj takes ṣirr/ṣirra as intense cold
Ibn al-Anbārī records three views: cold; sound and movement; and — reported from Ibn ʿAbbās — fire
A ḥadīth forbids locusts killed by the ṣirr, i.e. by cold
the root belongs to the category of letter-substitution (ibdāl) — the ṣād here standing in for a sīn
it means "the road/path."
Shāhid: Ibn Aḥmar, "clamorous of voice … the swooping falcon has no hope of her."
the returning or turning-back of a thing
turning (people) back: ṣaraftu al-qawm ("I turned the people back") and they inṣarafū (turned back / departed)
al-ṣarf in the Qur'an: repentance (tawba) — because through it a person is brought back from the rank of the sinners
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's own gloss of Qur'anic ṣarf

highlights.text: the line "O sons of Ghudāna, you are neither gold nor ṣarīf but earthenware,"
"cutting" (al-qaṭʿ). Every sense below is a variety of something being cut, cut off
al-ṣirām: the season for cutting date-clusters; aṣrama al-nakhl, "the palms became ready for harvest."
He cites the Qur'an, {so it became like al-ṣarīm} [68:20], glossing it himself as "it burned and turned black like the night"
For the "dawn" sense he quotes a verse of Bishr describing darkness clearing "from its ṣarīmah."
Cited in a proverb from the poet Bishr ("ṣurām has been milked"), meaning things have reached their worst
Ibn Fāris treats ṣ-r-r as having four roots, plus two words he cannot fit into them.
Iṣrār, resolve: he places it here because resolving on something and being fully set on it are one
Ṣirr is cold that harms plants, and the chill of a cold wind.
Ṣarra is intense shouting; the cricket's ṣarīr and the akhṭab's ṣarṣara.
Imruʾ al-Qays describes a herd's laggards "in a ṣarra that did not scatter".
as in al-Nābigha's "grey-haired monk … a ṣarūra given to devotion"
A ḥadīth says "there is no ṣarūra in Islam".
the name passed to the person who has not made the ḥajj
ṣarkha is the loud cry uttered in fright or at a disaster
ṣārikh and ṣarīkh are given as the one who calls for aid
highlights.note: ṣarīkh, 1x, a responder to a cry

highlights.text: "I am no muṣrikh of yours, nor are you muṣrikhs of mine." Abū al-Haytham glosses: "I am not your helper."
istaṣrakhanī fa-aṣrakhtuhu: "he sought my help and I helped him."
iṣṭarakha al-qawm, taṣārakhū, istaṣrakhū: they called out for help.
Zuhayr: "When we hear a crier for help, lean grey-flanked mounts race with us toward his voice."
In a report about Ibn ʿUmar, ustuṣrikha ("he was called out to") over his wife Ṣafiyya
A report has the Prophet rising at night on hearing the voice of "the ṣārikh," meaning the rooster
